planting.note: Plant grafted container trees in spring once frost danger has passed, in full sun and well-drained soil, and shield young trees through their first winters.

directions: Gainesville is a pure Mexican-race avocado that takes its name from a long-lived seedling tree that grew for decades outside a University of Florida building in Gainesville, demonstrating this cultivar's ability to survive occasional hard freezes well north of the traditional Florida avocado belt. Plant grafted trees in full sun and well-drained soil, and protect young trees through their first few winters until the root system matures. The oval, thin-skinned fruit stays green even when ripe and carries a proportionally large seed, with good but unremarkable flavor compared to commercial Guatemalan and hybrid types. Because it has fruited reliably across most seasons in University of Florida cold-hardiness trials, Gainesville is a reasonable dooryard choice for Gulf Coast growers who prioritize proven cold tolerance over fruit size.

common_name: Topa Topa Avocado (Historic Cold-Hardy Mexican-Race Avocado)

planting.note: Plant grafted container trees in spring once frost danger has passed, in full sun and well-drained soil, and protect young trees over their first winters.

directions: Topa Topa is one of the oldest named Mexican-race avocado selections, grown from a seedling near Ojai, California in the early twentieth century and later used widely as a parent and seedling rootstock for the California avocado industry, including early Hass plantings. The tree is vigorous and notably cold-tolerant for an avocado, shrugging off brief freezes that would damage Guatemalan or West Indian types. Fruit is small to medium, elongated and pear-shaped, with thin, dark purple-black skin and a waxy bloom, and flesh quality is only fair, so most growers today value this cultivar more for its hardiness than for eating quality. Give it full sun, well-drained soil, and winter protection while young, as with other Mexican-race avocados grown outside the traditional citrus belt.

planting.note: Plant grafted container trees in spring once frost danger has passed, in full sun and well-drained soil, and protect young trees through their first winters.

directions: Puebla is a historic pure Mexican-race avocado introduced to Southern California in the early twentieth century from the Mexican state it is named for, and was once prized as one of the best-flavored of the early Mexican imports used to build the California avocado industry. The fruit is small, with thin, smooth, nearly black skin that is often eaten along with the rich, creamy flesh. Wildfire losses in Southern California nearly wiped out the variety decades ago, and it survives today mainly in germplasm collections, though grafted trees occasionally reach specialty growers. Like other Mexican-race selections, Puebla tolerates occasional hard freezes better than Guatemalan or West Indian avocados, making it worth trying in protected zone 8b-9 Gulf Coast sites, though young trees still need winter protection.
